newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aborigines say land at heart of racial harmony.
newsitem.headline: Aborigines say land at heart of racial harmony.

text.p: An historic Aboriginal conference aimed at repairing black-white relations ended on Wednesday warning that racial harmony could not be achieved without an end to Australia's 200-year-old land conflict.

But in closing speeches, Aboriginal leaders said they feared Australia's conservative government lacked the commitment to achieve racial reconciliation by the centenary of Australia's nationhood in four years.
"I don't think we in Australia have the leadership to take us to reconciliation in 2001," said Noel Pearson, legal adviser to the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission.
"There is a pressing need for a moral or philosophical lobotomy or heart transplant on the part of our national leadership," Pearson said.
The 2,000 delegates attending the Aboriginal Reconciliation Convention called on Prime Minister John Howard to abandon his plan to effectively extinguish native title on farm land.

Ever since European settlement in 1788, white and black Australia have fought over land, with earlier settlers shooting and poisoning Aborgines and taking their land and Aborigines burning homesteads and murdering settlers.

Aborigines only won native land title in 1993 but Howard has warned that up to 78 percent of Australia's 7.68 million square km (2.96 million square miles) could ultimately be affected by native title claims.

The land issue topped a string of resolutions which also called for changes to the constitution to protect native languages and culture and raised the possibility of reserved parliamentary seats for Aborigines.

Unlike the U.S. constitution, the Australian constitution sets out primarily the role of government, not individual rights. There are some 300,000 Aborigines in Australia's 18 million population, but no Aboriginal parliamentarians.
"Without coexistence there can be no reconciliation. Land should be really seen as a potential bridge and not a point of conflict," former pastoralist Rick Farley told the conference.
"The simple reality is that land is absolutely essential to Aboriginal lore and culture, so while there is an Aboriginal culture there will be a land agenda."

The conference also called for an end to racism in Australia. Independent politician Pauline Hanson has sparked a bitter race debate, calling for cuts to Aboriginal welfare spending, claiming Aborigines receive preferential treatment.

"We need to ensure that when the insidious evil of racism and hatred raises its head, that we will be mature enough to recognise it and return it to the pits from where it came," said Pat Dodson, chairman of the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation.
